cues.text: A Council Convoked Twice
In keeping with the Council of Constance's decree Frequens requiring regular general councils, Pope Martin V summoned a new council to meet at Basel in Switzerland, though he died before it opened.
His successor, Eugene IV , confirmed the convocation but soon grew alarmed at the council's direction.
Dominated by lower clergy and driven by strong conciliarist sentiment, the Basel assembly began asserting authority over the pope himself.
In Eugene's judgment, it was drifting toward outright rebellion against papal authority.
Eugene attempted to dissolve the council in 1431 and relocate it to Bologna.
The Basel fathers refused to disperse, continuing to meet in open defiance and eventually electing their own rival pope, Felix V , in 1439—the last antipope in Church history.
The Move to Ferrara and Florence
Seeking to outflank the rebellious Basel assembly and pursue a project close to his heart — reunion with the Greek Church — Eugene IV summoned a rival continuation of the council to Ferrara in 1438.

There, he could personally negotiate with representatives of the Byzantine Emperor John VIII Palaiologos , who arrived in person with the Patriarch of Constantinople and a large delegation of Greek theologians.
An outbreak of plague forced a further transfer to Florence in January 1439, where the council's most significant achievements were reached.
After months of detailed theological debate — particularly over the filioque and the nature of purgatory — the Greek delegation agreed to a formula of union.
Led by the eloquent Cardinal Bessarion , it did so on July 6, 1439 , when the decree Laetentur Caeli proclaimed the reunion of the Greek and Latin Churches.
A Broader Reunion
The Council of Florence did not stop with the Greeks.
In the years that followed, similar decrees of union were negotiated and proclaimed with representatives of the Armenian , Coptic , and other Eastern Christian communities.
On paper, Florence became the broadest ecumenical reunion the Catholic Church achieved with the separated Eastern churches in the medieval period.

The council's decree for the Armenians, Exsultate Deo , also produced an influential summary of Catholic sacramental theology, listing and describing the seven sacraments in a systematic form that shaped catechesis for centuries afterward.
Union Unravels
As at Second Lyon a century and a half earlier, the union proclaimed at Florence rested on fragile foundations.
The Byzantine clergy and laity who had not traveled to Italy overwhelmingly rejected the agreement their delegates had signed.
When Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 , the union that might have brought Western military aid to the beleaguered Byzantine capital had already collapsed in practice.
Most of the Greek population saw Turkish rule as preferable to submission to Rome and unmourned the union.
The rival Basel assembly, meanwhile, steadily lost support as Eugene IV's Ferrara-Florence council demonstrated its greater legitimacy and achievements.
Felix V eventually resigned his antipapal claim in 1449.
The remnant of the Basel council dissolved itself shortly after, ending the conciliarist challenge to papal authority in dramatic and decisive fashion.
Legacy
The Council of Basel-Ferrara-Florence stands as a pivotal, two-sided episode.
At Basel, it marked conciliarism’s high-water mark and ultimate defeat as a serious rival to papal supremacy within the Latin Church.
At Ferrara-Florence, it was the medieval papacy’s most ambitious and theologically thorough attempt at healing the schism with the East.

Though the Eastern unions did not endure, the council's Florentine decrees on the procession of the Holy Spirit, purgatory, and the sacraments remain cited points of reference in Catholic-Orthodox theological dialogue to the present day.
